lines.text: In early 2020, this was a river, at the bottom of a canyon.
Six years later, it's a lake more than 200 km long.
It sits in Ethiopia, 14 km from the border with Sudan.
2,500 km downstream, Egypt's leaders have called it an existential threat.
Ethiopia's prime minister says it was built to light up homes, not to harm anyone.
This is the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. To understand why it has two of Africa's biggest nations at odds, you have to follow the water.
On a map, the Nile seems to begin at Lake Victoria, in the heart of East Africa.
From there, it runs north for more than 6,000 km, through eleven countries.
That branch, the White Nile, is the longer one. But it's not where most of the water comes from.
In Khartoum, it meets a second river, coming down from the Ethiopian highlands. The Blue Nile.
In flood season you can see them meet: the White Nile, wide and pale, and the Blue Nile, brown with mud from the mountains.
Every summer, monsoon rain falls on the highlands, and the Blue Nile swells into a torrent.
Together with two smaller rivers from Ethiopia, it supplies about 85% of the water that reaches Egypt.
And Egypt, which gets almost no rain, takes nearly all of its fresh water from the Nile.
For most of the last century, the rules for this water were written without Ethiopia.
In 1959, Egypt and Sudan signed an agreement dividing the river between themselves.
Egypt would take 55.5 billion cubic metres a year. Sudan, 18.5.
Ethiopia, where most of that water starts, had no share, and no seat at the table.
Egypt still treats that treaty, and an older one from 1929, as the basis of its rights.
That older deal, signed under British colonial rule, even gave Egypt the right to object to projects upstream.
Ethiopia rejects both, as deals made about its river, without it.
Now look at the same region at night.
Egypt's river glows. The Ethiopian highlands are almost dark.
Ethiopia has more people than Egypt. But in 2023, nearly half of them still had no electricity.
In 2011, Ethiopia began building its answer, on the Blue Nile, close to the Sudanese border.
It paid for most of it itself. The government sold bonds to its own people, and workers gave part of their salaries.
The result: a wall of concrete 145 metres high, and almost 2 km long, across the canyon.
Its turbines can produce 5,150 megawatts. The largest hydropower plant in Africa, and more than twice the Aswan High Dam.
For many Ethiopians, it's more than a power plant. It's a symbol of what the country can do on its own.
A hydropower dam doesn't use up a river. The water runs through the turbines, and on downstream.
The problem is filling it. To make a lake, you have to hold water back, and every cubic metre held back is water that doesn't reach Egypt that year.
Ethiopia started filling in July 2020, without an agreement with Egypt or Sudan.
This is the reservoir, photographed by Landsat every dry season since.
Early 2021: about 175 square kilometres of water.
By the end of 2022, almost 700.
And by January 2026, more than 1,500 square kilometres. A lake about the size of London.
Behind the dam, the water climbed 140 metres up the canyon walls, one rainy season at a time.
Full, it holds 74 billion cubic metres. More than Egypt's entire yearly share under the 1959 treaty.
All the while, the talks went nowhere. A declaration of principles in 2015. Talks in Washington in 2020. Debates at the UN Security Council.
In December 2023, Egypt declared the negotiations over.
So far, Egypt has not run short. The filling years were mostly wet ones, and Egypt had its own reserve: Lake Nasser, behind the Aswan High Dam.
Egypt's fear is the dry years. In the 1980s, a run of weak floods drained Lake Nasser close to its limit.
If a drought like that comes again, who holds water back, and who lets it go?
Egypt wants the answer written into a binding agreement. Ethiopia says a dam on its own land shouldn't need permission from downstream.
Ethiopia also argues the dam helps downstream: a deep reservoir in the cool highlands loses less water to evaporation than a lake in the desert, and a steadier river means fewer floods in Sudan.
Sudan is caught in between. It could gain steadier water and fewer floods, but it lives closest to the dam, and it has raised concerns about the dam's safety.
Underneath it all is a bigger shift. For the first time, the flow of the Blue Nile is controlled upstream, by Ethiopia.
That shift was tested in the autumn of 2025, just weeks after the dam was formally inaugurated.
Heavy rain fell on the highlands, and downstream, the river rose. Near Khartoum, more than a thousand families were forced from their homes.
Egypt called it a man-made flood, caused by sudden releases from the dam.
Ethiopia said the opposite: that the dam had held water back, and without it, the damage would have been far worse.
Sudanese officials also pointed to the White Nile, and to infrastructure damaged by war.
Without an agreement to share data on how the dam is run, each country tells its own version.
In November 2026, Egypt and Sudan again demanded a binding legal agreement. And Ethiopia is planning more dams on the Blue Nile.
Remember that line of light across Egypt? It starts here, as rain, on the dark highlands of Ethiopia.
One river. Two great dams. And still no agreement on who decides how much of it flows.
